title: GA-SAM: Gradient-Strength based Adaptive Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Improved Generalization
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
publication_status_observed: arXiv preprint arXiv:2210.06895v1 [cs.LG] 13 Oct 2022; venue listed as EMNLP in header
main_claims: Distribution shifts between training and test sets can be equivalently treated as virtual parameter corruptions near corresponding minima, providing a direct theoretical justification for why flat minima generalise better.
The optimal strength of parameter corruption should be proportional to gradient strength (inversely), motivating gradient-strength based adaptive corruption scales in SAM.
GA-SAM, which uses layer-wise gradient-strength adaptive corruption scales with multi-step risk minimisation, outperforms standard SAM and its variants on NLP tasks.
methodology: The authors derive a theoretical framework (Theorems 1-2, Propositions 1-3) showing that a small distribution shift induces a parameter shift proportional to the inverse of the loss Hessian multiplied by the expected gradient under the distribution shift. Under the Fisher information matrix assumption, this yields an inverse relationship between corruption strength and gradient strength. GA-SAM implements layer-wise adaptive scales T(i) = sqrt(n(i)) / ||g(i)||_2 / sqrt(n) in a multi-step SAM framework and is evaluated on CNN (IMDB), LSTM (PTB-LM), and Transformer (En-Vi, De-En) benchmarks.
key_results: GA-SAM achieves ACC 86.11 (+1.69 over baseline) on IMDB and PPL 84.52 (-2.18) on PTB-LM, outperforming SAM (+0.33, +2.96) and all other adaptive SAM variants.
GA-SAM achieves BLEU 31.15 (+0.55) on En-Vi and 35.95 (+0.54) on De-En, surpassing SAM (+0.19, +0.20) and FreeLB (+0.31, +0.08).
Top-50 Hessian eigenvalues are lower for GA-SAM than baselines (Fig. 3), and parameter robustness under L2 and L-inf corruptions is improved (Table 4), confirming flatter minima.
limitations: Hyperparameter tuning for epsilon is time-consuming and environmentally costly, requiring grid search over many orders of magnitude.
The theoretical framework assumes mu-strongly convex loss locally near the minimum, which does not hold globally for deep networks.
Experiments are on NLP tasks only; generalisation to vision or OOD settings (e.g., CIFAR-C) is not tested.
relevance_to_rq: This paper's theoretical framework—that distribution shifts manifest as parameter corruptions, and flat minima resist these—directly connects flatness to OOD generalisation in a principled way. While the setting is NLP rather than vision corruptions, the theory underpins why SAM-style optimisers should help on CIFAR-C benchmarks, which is the RQ's empirical domain.
